https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgk4.text: By Matt Murphy BBC Verify Published 2 hours ago Russian and Malian troops fighting against a rebel offensive in northern Mali have been resupplied with a vast number of military vehicles that appear to have been delivered by a sanctioned cargo ship, BBC Verify has found. A large column of armoured vehicles were seen arriving in the capital Bamako in verified footage broadcast by Malian state TV on 25 July. Reporters said the convoy had travelled from LomÃ© port in Togo. A sanctioned Russian cargo ship, Mikhail Britnev, docked in LomÃ© on 9 July, according to ship tracking data reviewed by BBC Verify. Satellite images appear to show that the ship was carrying the kind of trucks, armoured personnel carriers and light infantry vehicles seen in Bamako, according to experts. Ship tracking data shows that the Mikhail Britnev left Russia's Baltiysk port on 18 June and moved through the North Sea before entering the English Channel. BBC Verify understands that the vessel was escorted through the Channel by a Russian Ropucha-class warship. The UK's Ministry of Defence declined to comment. Experts say the deliveries signify that the Kremlin is doubling down on its support for Mali's ruling junta, which has been rocked by the success of a rebel offensive led by the Jihadist group Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and Tuareg separatists. The advance has seized large swathes of territory in the north. The Kremlin has backed the Mali military government since French forces withdrew from the country in 2022 , receiving cash payments and preferential access to mines and gold deposits in return. At first the Russian mercenary group Wagner was deployed, but its operations have since been taken over by Africa Corps, which falls under Russia's defence ministry. While BBC Verify has previously confirmed footage showing the unit carrying out air strikes against the rebel forces , the Africa Corps has struggled to halt their advance across the north of the country. But Charlie Werb, an analyst with Aldebaran Threat Consultants, said the new shipment could help Malian and Russian forces to build up enough strength to launch offensives into areas which have fallen to the rebels. The Mikhail Britnev was sanctioned by the US in 2024. Tracking data shows it switched off its transponder after passing through the Channel two weeks ago, and only reappeared when preparing to dock in Togo. It was carrying a variety of military vehicles - including general purpose trucks, BTR-style armoured personnel carriers and light-infantry vehicles - according to experts who analysed satellite photos taken before it left Baltiysk port. According to Malian state TV, the vehicles were then transported across Togo and through Burkina Faso - which is also ruled by a military junta backed by Moscow. The government in Togo has been deepening ties with the Kremlin and signed a military cooperation agreement with Moscow late last year. The vehicles could be used for a mix of logistics and planning manoeuvres, as well combat operations, analysts at the defence intelligence firm Janes said. BBC Verify understands that Baltiysk port has been the staging point for several ships exporting military materials to West Africa. The bulk carrier Sabetta was tracked after loading what appeared to be military vehicles at the port in February. It docked at Conakry in Guinea, a port long associated with weapons transfers from Russia to its regional allies in West Africa. Another tanker, which did not appear on ship tracking data, was also seen loading military vehicles at Baltiysk on 6 June. Mali's military junta has suffered several battlefield setbacks in recent weeks. Rebel fighters have carried out sustained attacks on the northern town of Anefis, with clashes also reported near Niono and other parts of central Mali. Amnesty International on Wednesday called for a war crimes investigation into what it said were the summary executions of at least 19 Malian soldiers after an ambush earlier this month. But Werb said the delivery showed that the Kremlin was digging in to defend its allied junta. "The Kremlin has maintained steady military support since the conflict entered a new phase on 25 April by bringing in fresh forces, weapons, and equipment," he said. "The delivery highlights that despite recent setbacks, Mali remains central to Russia's strategy in Africa, and the Africa Corps is a key pillar in Bamako's fight against militant groups." https://www.politico.eu/article/man-inju.text: One man was injured in a shooting in Brussels’ Saint-Gilles municipality Saturday evening, just a day after gunmen targeted a police station in Anderlecht. Saint-Gilles Mayor Jean Spinette told Belga news agency the victim didn’t suffer life-threatening injuries and linked the incident to narcotics-related crime. The shots were fired on a square known as “place des Deux Bancs,” associated with drug trafficking. The attack comes one day after shooters carrying a heavy weapon targeted a police station in another Brussels municipality, Anderlecht, before fleeing on an e-scooter. Advertisement Advertisement The violence marked “yet another wake-up call” for the Belgian capital, the region’s Minister-President Boris Dilliès reacted on X . “We will not let organized crime take over our city,” he added. Dilliès said his government was taking measures to address the violence, including by appointing a Brussels commissioner for drugs, who will take on the role from September, and by restricting the use of e-scooters, which he said “unfortunately, are often used by criminals.” The city’s top prosecutor Julien Moinil said that, given the target of Friday night’s shooting, “there is a clear intent to undermine authority” — but he added that “they will not succeed.” He explained that a lot of shootings are ordered from inside prison, calling for secure zones where phones cannot operate. Brussels recorded 57 shootings in the first seven months of 2026. Two people were killed and 21 injured, according to VRT .

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Baby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April. Photograph: Raoul Dixon/North News/North News & Pictures Ltd View image in fullscreen Baby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April. Photograph: Raoul Dixon/North News/North News & Pictures Ltd North of England Baby found wrapped in 1910 newspaper was killed with twine, UK inquest concludes ‘Terrible thing’ happened to infant boy found under the floorboards at a house in Bishop Auckland, says coroner Mark Brown North of England correspondent Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.06 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A baby boy who was found with twine looped and knotted round his neck and wrapped in a 116-year-old newspaper was unlawfully killed, a coroner has concluded. Crispin Oliver on Thursday said the child, known only as Baby Auckland, had been garotted by an unknown person. He said it was an “unusual case, legally and evidentially”. The whole story, he added, was “very sad and singular”. Oliver said: “Clearly, this was a terrible thing that happened to a defenceless infant. It happened in our community. But it happened over a century ago, and it is heartwarming how the public and individuals in this community have stepped up to do the right thing by Baby Auckland.” The inquest heard that the skeletal remains of the baby had been found during renovations on the second floor of a late 19th-century house in Bishop Auckland, County Durham, on 29 July 2024. They were found by the house owner, Peter Moody, while he was laying a new floor. In a statement he said he had made the discovery when he lifted up a floorboard. He contacted the county council, unsure of whether he needed to call the police. DCI Mel Sutherland told the inquest he had been on duty in Bishop Auckland when he was alerted to the discovery of skeletal remains in a town centre house. After they were confirmed as human, he supervised the sealing of the house to keep it forensically sterile, while a forensic anthropologist was contacted. That scientist, Dr Micol Zuppello, travelled up that evening and spent two days at the house investigating. The baby’s skeleton was mostly complete, the inquest in Crook heard, bar a missing toe tip. The remains were partly mummified. Carbon dating could conclusively establish only that the baby died between the 17th century and 1955. A postmortem of the skeleton was carried out by Zupello and Dr Louise Mulcahy, a Home Office pathologist for north-east England based at the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle. Mulcahy said the baby had been 38-40 weeks, with no signs of traumatic injury, and had twine looped around his neck. She said it had been looped around the neck three times, knotted, and then looped again. View image in fullscreen PCSOs and a forensics officer outside the building in Bishop Auckland in 2024, after the discovery was made. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA It was not possible to say, she added, if it had been tight or loose. The medical cause of death, she said, was “unascertained”. The skeleton was too old to be able to confirm or refute the presence of natural disease, she said. In the absence of soft tissue it was not possible, the inquest heard, to say if there had been any assault or trauma. Equally, it was not possible to say with any certainty if the baby had been stillborn or not. Oliver said police had “had to think laterally” during their investigation. He praised Sutherland for “leaving no stone unturned”. Sutherland described some of the techniques they had used to investigate further, including DNA testing. All were inconclusive. He said the newspaper was very brown, but articles could be seen. It was called The Umpire and dated June 1910. Sutherland said that in 1911 census data, the building was described as dining rooms, meaning “a cafe-type establishment”. A public appeal was made for people who thought they might be related to come forward. Two sisters came forward who believed they were related to a servant at the house, but DNA testing revealed no match. During the whole investigation, Sutherland said, there had been “very little to go on”. Oliver asked if the twine might have been used for a religious artefact, but nothing like that had been found, Sutherland said. There was also no evidence to suggest any link to midwifery practices of the time. A knot specialist could not be used, the inquest heard, because the nearest person was in the Netherlands and would have been too expensive for this type of investigation. Baby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April this year, with professionals involved giving their services for free. Sutherland said it had been two years of investigating, “challenging and frustrating at times, but heartwarming to see the send-off he got at the end”. https://www.politico.eu/article/send-rej.text: ATHENS — Greece is spearheading a group of five EU countries pushing for migrants who have been denied the right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries such as Rwanda from as early as next year. Greece’s Migration Minister Thanos Plevris said in an interview that by the first half of 2027, the so-called Core Group of nations — Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands — aims to have a pilot project in place to send rejected asylum-seekers to designated countries outside the bloc. He added that the project should be fully operational by the second half of the year — coinciding with Greece taking over the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU in July. The intervention comes as Europe continues to grapple with a decade-long migration crisis which has galvanized support for populist-nationalist parties across the continent. Advertisement Advertisement Plevris emphasized that the plan does not entail establishing return facilities but rather designates return countries. “We’re not talking about centers, in the sense that someone whose asylum is rejected is sent to a closed facility in a third country,” he said. “If your asylum has been rejected, you will either return to your country of origin or to a third country outside the EU.” According to two EU diplomats familiar with the issue who were granted anonymity to discuss the matter freely, the first deal will be with Rwanda. Uganda and Uzbekistan are also reportedly under discussion as possible return countries. Plevris said the countries under consideration already have large migrant populations and camps to accommodate them, adding that the Core Group nations “are open to whatever framework the countries there want — whether they want to talk about camps, or broader integration programs.” Rwanda has been at the center of various offshore migration plans. In 2022, the U.K. announced a controversial multimillion-pound deal with Kigali to deport asylum-seekers to the country to have their claims processed. The scheme was abandoned after years of legal challenges . The timetable proposed by Plevris might be ambitious, given that several crucial elements of the agreement remain up in the air. The minister said members of the Core Group are currently in discussions with international organizations to establish monitoring processes that would ensure human rights are respected in third countries to which migrants will be deported . “Obviously, we’re not going to transfer this authority elsewhere,” he added. “We want to have the expertise and the presence of international organizations, but the responsibility lies with the five countries, jointly.” Advertisement Advertisement The financing of the plan — an issue which can be contentious with voters — would also have to come from the Core Group. “We want to have a financially realistic project,” Plevris said, adding that members of the group want the Commission to eventually have an active role in the process. The minister acknowledged that the plan would not lead to huge numbers of migrants being outsourced to third countries. “In reality, it is another means of exerting pressure that could increase voluntary returns,” he said. “It’s an unprecedented undertaking. Even though other countries have attempted something similar in the past, this is the first time it’s being attempted since the EU regulation was passed.” On Thursday, at a meeting of EU interior ministers, Plevris will also submit Greece’s plan to deal with emergency migratory pressures — temporarily suspending asylum applications for newly arrived people. Greece’s Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis first presented this idea in an Op-Ed published on POLITICO after tens of thousands of migrants crossed the border into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta. “The EU migration will only work when Europe’s migration flows are managed,” Plevris said, adding that the bloc needs a mechanism to deal with emergencies. Greece has been repeatedly accused of violating EU regulations for alleged illegal pushbacks of migrants. “Greece protects its borders in accordance with international law, and it says frankly that it will not apologize to anyone for protecting its borders,” the minister added. Plevris, who has expressed hard-line views on migration, has expressed his support and admiration for U.S. President Donald Trump’s approach on the issue. “He gave the momentum that led to a change in migration policy, and essentially helped many groups —including us — who believed in a stricter immigration policy to see it materialize,” said Plevris. He also confirmed that European prosecutors are investigating how Greece used EU funds to construct migrant camps . “We have been asked for data and information regarding audits and we have provided them, but there have been no further developments,” he added. https://www.genazym.com/auction/628-perf.text: First Chassidic Sefer Ever Printed Sefer Yesod of the Baal Shem Tov’s Teachings Toldos Yaakov Yosef Koritz, 1780. First Edition. The sefer yesod of Chassidus – a commentary on the Chamisha Chumshei Torah by Rabbi Yaakov Yosef HaKohen of Polonne, the Baal Shem Tov’s closest disciple and the first and greatest disseminator of the teachings of the Baal Shem Tov. It is therefore no surprise that the publication of this sefer intensified the struggle against the emerging Chassidic movement. It is alluded to in the Vilna ban against Chassidus, fiercely attacked in the polemical works Zemir Aritzim and Shever Poshim, and was even publicly burned in the city of Brody. Exceptionally rare in such fine condition. Bound in a new, elegant leather binding, befitting this important and distinguished sefer.
